facts.statement: Cardabiodon lived between 95 and 91 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Cardabiodon (; meaning 'Cardabia tooth') is an extinct genus of large mackerel shark that lived about 95 to 91 million years ago (Ma) during the Cenomanian to Turonian of the Late Cretaceous.

facts.statement: Cardabiodon was likely an apex predator that hunted plesiosaurs, ichthyosaurs, and large fish using its robust teeth and fast swimming.
facts.quote: It may have been an apex predator in its ecosystem and likely used its large, robust teeth and fast swimming capabilities to prey on a variety of marine animals including plesiosaurs, ichthyosaurs, and other large fish.

facts.statement: Cardabiodon possessed a very heavy and stocky body structure.
facts.quote: Cardabiodon also had a very heavy and stocky body.

facts.statement: Cardabiodon individuals were born between 41 and 76 cm long and reached sexual maturity at five to seven years of age.
facts.quote: At birth, Cardabiodon individuals measured between 41-76 cm in length and reached sexual maturity at around five to seven years of age

facts.statement: The genus Cardabiodon was described by Mikael Siverson in 1999 from fossils found in Western Australia.
facts.quote: Cardabiodon was described from an associated fossil discovered in the Southern Carnarvon Basin of the Gearle Siltstone which is located within Cardabia, a cattle station in Western Australia, by paleontologist Mikael Siverson, who published his findings in 1999.

facts.statement: The second species, C. venator, was described in 2005 by Siverson and Johan Lindgren based on 37 teeth found in Montana.
facts.quote: Six years later, in 2005, Siverson and his Swedish colleague Johan Lindgren described the second species C. venator from specimens consisting of a total of 37 teeth recovered from a locality of the Fairport Member of the Carlile Shale near Mosby, Montana

facts.statement: Cardabiodon skin was covered in teardrop-shaped scales with 6 to 8 parallel grooves and kneels.
facts.quote: The skin of Cardabiodon was covered by teardrop-shaped enameloid placoid scales clad with 6–8 parallel grooves that each possessed kneels.

facts.statement: The specialized scales of Cardabiodon suggest it was capable of fast swimming to pursue lively prey.
facts.quote: Scales with grooves and kneels are efficient in hydrodynamic drag-reduction and are correlated with the swimming ability of the shark possessing them, being common in fast-swimming sharks like lamnids. This means it is likely that Cardabiodon too was capable of fast swimming and thus pursuit of lively prey.

facts.statement: Cardabiodon had a rigid, spindle-shaped vertebral column that was poorly flexible but efficient for fast swimming.
facts.quote: The vertebral column was rigid and spindle-shaped, which would be poorly flexible but efficient for fast swimming.

facts.statement: Cardabiodon had a heterodontic dental structure with many different tooth morphologies.
facts.quote: Cardabiodon possessed the basic dental characteristics for a mackerel shark. Its dental structure was heterodontic, meaning that there were many tooth morphologies present.

facts.statement: Cardabiodon teeth featured bilabial roots, robust crowns, large tooth necks, nonserrated edges, and lateral cusplets.
facts.quote: Diagnostic features of Cardabiodon teeth include strongly bilabial roots, robust crowns that is either near-symmetrically erect or distally curved, visible and large tooth necks (bourlette), nonserrated cutting edges, and lateral cusplets.

facts.statement: The largest teeth of C. ricki measured up to 3.98 cm in slant height.
facts.quote: The largest tooth examples of C. ricki come from the holotype. Its anterior teeth measure up to 3.67 cm in maximum slant height, while the first few lower lateroposteriors are larger and measure up to 3.98 cm in maximum slant height.

facts.statement: The largest known tooth of C. venator measured 3.26 cm in slant height and was notably bulky and thick.
facts.quote: C. venator teeth are slightly smaller, with the largest known tooth discovered being an anterior measuring 3.26 cm in maximum slant height but are much more bulky and thicker instead.

facts.statement: Cardabiodon belongs to the unique family Cardabiodontidae and includes the species C. ricki and C. venator.
facts.quote: It is a member of the Cardabiodontidae, a family unique among mackerel sharks due to differing dental structures, and contains the two species C. ricki and C. venator.

facts.statement: Siverson concluded that the former taxon Cretolamna woodwardi likely represents two distinct genera, one of which is Cardabiodon.
facts.quote: He also found that the former Cr. woodwardi actually represents two distinct genera of sharks, which was also the likely case for Pseudoisurus tomosus- The first was C. ricki (which he already described using WAM.96.4.45), and the other was assigned the taxon Dwardius woodwardi.

facts.statement: Cardabiodon possessed a unique dental structure unlike any other known living or extinct shark.
facts.quote: The dental structure of Cardabiodon is unique and incomparable with any other known extant or extinct shark.

facts.statement: In Cardabiodon, lower jaw tooth size abruptly increased to peak at the first lateroposterior tooth, contrary to the gradual decrease seen in other mackerel sharks.
facts.quote: In the lower jaw, tooth size abruptly increases and peaks at the first lateroposterior tooth.

facts.statement: The bite circumference of the Cardabiodon ricki holotype's lower jaw was measured at 746 mm.
facts.quote: The lower jaw bite circumference of the C. ricki holotype was measured to be 746 mm.

facts.statement: Siverson established the family Cardabiodontidae to include Cardabiodon and the extinct Cenozoic shark Parotodus due to their unique dental structures.
facts.quote: To reflect the unique dental structure of Cardabiodon, Siverson erected the family Cardabiodontidae and placed the taxon, along with an extinct Cenozoic shark, Parotodus, in it.

facts.statement: The Late Cretaceous shark Dwardius, which has teeth very similar to Cardabiodon, is also placed within the family Cardabiodontidae.
facts.quote: Another Late Cretaceous shark, Dwardius, whose teeth are very similar with those of Cardabiodon, would also be placed within the family.

facts.statement: The phylogenetic placement of the family Cardabiodontidae remains uncertain and has not yet been established.
facts.quote: The phylogenetic placement of the Cardabiodontidae is uncertain and yet to be established.

facts.statement: Fossils of an early Cardabiodontid, including teeth and vertebrae, date to the Albian age (105 million years ago) and were found in the Toolebuc Formation in Queensland.
facts.quote: The most notable of them includes an associated set of teeth and very large vertebrae dated in the Albian age of 105 Ma from the Toolebuc Formation in Queensland

facts.statement: An early Cardabiodontid individual from the Albian age was estimated to reach a length of 8 to 9 meters.
facts.quote: that belonged to an individual that was estimated to measure 8-9 m in length.

facts.statement: Vertebrae of Cardabiodon ricki suggest that newborn individuals were between 41 and 76 cm in total length, which is smaller than the birth sizes of Cretoxyrhina mantelli and Archaeolamna kopingensis.
facts.quote: When compared with the ontogenetic records of Cretoxyrhina mantelli and Archaeolamna kopingensis, the vertebrae of C. ricki suggested that total length at birth was smaller than the two sharks at between 41-76 cm.

facts.statement: Three vertebral specimens of Cardabiodon ricki showed thirteen growth rings, indicating these individuals lived to approximately 13 years of age.
facts.quote: All three vertebral specimens showed thirteen growth rings, meaning that the individuals lived to around 13 years of age.

facts.statement: A 2010 study led by Todd D. Cook proposed that Cardabiodon and Dwardius might be synonymous genera, though Siverson expressed unlikeliness due to contradictory evolutionary trends.
facts.quote: There has been a proposal of a close relationship between the two, and the possibility of them being synonymous genera has been raised by a 2010 study led by paleontologist Todd D. Cook.

facts.statement: The genus Cardabiodon was named by Mikael Siverson in 1999.
facts.quote: Cardabiodon fue nombrado por Mikael Siverson en 1999.

facts.statement: Reconstructions of vertebrae and jaws suggest Cardabiodon reached a maximum size of 5.5 meters.
facts.quote: Según los estudios de reconstrucciones de vértebras y mandíbulas indican un tamaño superior de 5,5 metros.

facts.statement: Cardabiodon lived during the Late Cretaceous, specifically the Cenomanian and Turonian stages, approximately 99.7 to 94.3 million years ago.
facts.quote: Cardabiodon es un género representado por dos especies de tiburón cardabiodóntido, que vivieron a finales del período Cretácico, hace aproximadamente 99.7 a 94.3 millones de años, en el Cenomaniense y el Turoniense

facts.statement: Cardabiodon inhabited sea surface temperatures ranging from 17.5 to 24.2 degrees Celsius.
facts.quote: It has been determined that Cardabiodons sea surface temperature range was 17.5-24.2 C.

facts.statement: Most Cardabiodon fossils come from North America, specifically the southern half of the Western Interior Seaway.
facts.quote: The majority of its fossils are from North America. In North America, C. venator fossils are found mostly in the southern half of the Western Interior Seaway

facts.statement: The Carlile Shale near Mosby, Montana, has been identified as a nursery area for Cardabiodon due to the high prevalence of juvenile fossils.
facts.quote: An area of the Carlile Shale near Mosby, Montana, has been identified as a nursery site due to the rich prevalence of juvenile Cardabiodon fossils.

facts.statement: Like modern sharks, Cardabiodon utilized shallow nursery areas to protect its young from predators.
facts.quote: Cardabiodon made use of nursery areas to give birth to and raise young, which would ideally be shallow waters that provides protection from natural predators.

facts.statement: Fossils of Cardabiodon have been found in Canada, the midwestern United States, England, West Australia, and Kazakhstan.
facts.quote: Cardabiodon fossils have been found in Canada, the midwestern United States, England, West Australia, and Kazakhstan.

facts.statement: Cardabiodon fossils found between 40° and 60° paleolatitude suggest an antitropical distribution similar to modern porbeagle sharks.
facts.quote: It had been implied in the past that Cardabiodon may have had an antitropical distribution as these localities were between 40° and 60° paleolatitude

facts.quote: genus_authority: Siverson, 1999

facts.quote: type_species: Cardabiodon ricki

facts.statement: The genus Cardabiodon includes two species: the type species C. ricki and C. venator.
facts.quote: subdivision: C. ricki Siverson, 1999 (especie tipo) C. venator Siverson & Lindgren, 2005

facts.statement: The time range for the genus Cardabiodon is from the Cenomanian to the Santonian, spanning 100.5 to 83.6 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Cenomanian to Santonian (100.5 to 83.6 million years ago)

facts.statement: Research suggests Cardabiodon shifted its distribution farther north before the Cenomanian-Turonian Thermal Optimum (about 93 Ma) due to rising temperatures.
facts.quote: The study also found that the highest latitudinal fossils of Cardabiodon were dated just before the warmest period in the Late Cretaceous about 93 Ma known as the Cenomanian-Turonian Thermal Optimum, suggesting a shift in distribution farther north due to increasing temperatures and tropical environments.

facts.statement: It is proposed that Cardabiodon could migrate between hemispheres by crossing deeper, cooler waters.
facts.quote: It has been proposed that Cardabiodon may have been able to move from one hemisphere to the other by crossing deeper and thus cooler waters.

facts.statement: The hypothesis of inter-hemispheric migration is supported by the presence of Cardabiodon teeth in deep-water deposits near its lowest paleolatitude range.
facts.quote: Although no Cardabiodon fossils have been found outside its inferred range, this proposal is supported by the occurrence of Cardabiodon teeth in deep-water deposits around its lowest paleolatitudinal range.

facts.statement: Cardabiodon lived during the Cenomanian-Turonian Thermal Optimum, a time of significant biodiversity change and the radiation of new fauna like mosasaurs.
facts.quote: Cardabiodon was contemporaneous with the Cenomanian-Turonian Thermal Optimum, which led to a change in biodiversity and appearance and radiation of a new fauna like mosasaurs.

facts.statement: As a presumed apex predator, Cardabiodon likely preyed on various marine vertebrates coexisting in the Western Interior Seaway, including sharks, bony fish, seabirds, marine reptiles, and sea turtles.
facts.quote: Cenomanian localities in the Western Interior Seaway have yielded several marine vertebrates that coexisted with Cardabiodon, which the shark, presumably as an apex predator, may have preyed upon.

facts.statement: Benthic fauna was rare in the northern waters inhabited by Cardabiodon due to low oxygen levels from the Cenomanian-Turonian anoxic event, which caused the extinction of up to 27% of marine invertebrates.
facts.quote: Benthic faunae were rare around this time, especially in the more northern waters Cardabiodon inhabited. This was due mostly to lower oxygen levels caused by the Cenomanian-Turonian anoxic event which led to the extinction of as much as 27% of all marine invertebrates.
